title: Quantum erasure conversion: sense amps flag low-margin bits as erasures
idea: Neutral-atom quantum computers convert errors into erasures at known locations. Borrow that by adding a second, offset-threshold comparator to each sense amp, so any bit whose bitline differential falls below ~40 mV is flagged 'uncertain' and sent to the controller as a per-burst erasure mask on an extra pin. The controller runs erasure-aware Reed-Solomon decoding, which corrects about twice as many erasures as unknown errors for the same parity.
why: Retention-tail and VRT cells read with low margin before they actually flip. Erasure decoding lets the same 12.5% parity tolerate ~2x the raw weak-cell rate, which permits ~15-20% smaller Cs or 2-4x longer refresh (facts 1, 3).

title: KV-cache-grade rows: full cells for exponents, cheap cells for mantissas
idea: AI KV-caches and weights survive flipped low mantissa bits but not flipped exponents. Build a 'BF16-graded' region where hard-wired bit-lane routing places sign, exponent and high mantissa bits in standard ~5 fF cells on normal refresh. The 8 low mantissa bits go in half-height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) capacitors on a relaxed 256 ms refresh with no retention guarantee.
why: Half of the bits avoid the AR 60-75 capacitor and most refresh: ~20-30% less refresh energy and a cheaper capacitor module for AI memory, at <0.1% accuracy loss (facts 1, 3).

title: Reactor-style self-anneal: on-die heaters heal leakage-tail traps
idea: Radiation-damaged detectors and fusion-reactor sensors are recovered by thermal annealing. Embed polysilicon heater lines in the periphery stripes of each bank. During a scheduled window, after the bank's data has been migrated away, the heaters hold the array at ~250 C for minutes to passivate the interface and oxide traps that create GIDL and VRT tail cells. An on-die tail monitor decides when a bank needs annealing.
why: Tail leakage cells (≤13 fA) set the 64 ms refresh. Periodically resetting the aging-driven growth of the tail could keep refresh intervals 2-4x longer over life and cut in-field weak-cell repairs (fact 3).

title: Satellite scrub-per-refresh: ECC engines inside every sense-amp stripe
idea: Satellites crossing the South Atlantic Anomaly scrub memory faster than upsets can accumulate. Put a small SEC-DED engine in each subarray's sense-amp stripe, so every refresh of a row reads, corrects and writes back corrected data instead of re-amplifying whatever is there. Single flips are cleared every 64 ms, so two independent errors never pile up in one codeword.
why: Double errors from accumulation are what force worst-case cell specs. Correcting at every refresh allows ~10x higher raw single-bit error rates for the same uncorrectable rate, which accepts weaker capacitors and leakier tails at a few percent extra periphery (facts 1, 3).

title: Downhole elastic ECC: parity grows as the die heats
idea: Downhole tools at 200 C trade capacity for survival. Tie on-die ECC strength to a junction-temperature sensor: rows step from a (136,128) SEC code to (144,128) DEC to (160,128) as temperature rises. The extra parity comes from a reserved top-of-memory region that the OS gives up through a memory-balloon driver; when the die is cool, that reserve is usable capacity.
why: Retention halves every ~10 C, so specs written for 95 C over-design cells for the ~95% of time a die spends near 50 C. Elastic redundancy lets cells be specified at typical temperature, roughly a 1.5-2x looser retention spec (fact 3).

title: Subsea-repeater cold spare: an unpowered extra die per stack
idea: Undersea cable repeaters carry unpowered cold spares through a 25-year unserviceable life. Add one unpowered DRAM die to each HBM/3DS stack, with a base-die crossbar that moves a degrading die's contents to the spare and remaps its channels once its corrected-error rate crosses a threshold. Powered-off silicon accumulates no BTI, hot-carrier or hammer stress.
why: Stacks can ship with lower-margin dies, and end-of-life die failures become transparent swaps. That raises effective HBM stack yield and lifetime by ~10-20% for ~6-12% extra silicon (fact 6).

title: Cryo-control DRAM: shallow capacitors because 77 K kills leakage
idea: Quantum-computer control electronics run at 4-77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by ~10^6 and retention stretches to hours. Design a die that only runs in liquid nitrogen, with 0.5-1 fF capacitors (AR ~10 or planar) and no refresh circuitry, for sealed LN2-immersion AI racks. Reliability comes from temperature instead of capacitor height.
why: Removes the AR 60-75 capacitor and refresh (facts 1, 3): a ~5-6x shorter capacitor etch and fewer steps. The cost is LN2 cooling energy, partly offset by lower wire resistance and leakage.

title: Miner-style undervolting: per-bank array voltage servoed by live ECC counts
idea: Crypto miners undervolt memory until errors just begin to appear. Give each bank its own array-voltage regulator and a closed loop that lowers VARY in 10 mV steps while that bank's on-die ECC corrected-error rate stays under budget, and backs off immediately on a burst. Banks with strong cells may settle near 0.8 V instead of ~1.05 V.
why: Array CV^2 energy is pinned at the voltage floor (fact 10). Running each bank at its real margin saves ~25-35% of array and refresh energy, and lets parts with weaker banks still meet energy specs.

title: CERN trigger-buffer logic: declared-lifetime rows skip refresh entirely
idea: LHC trigger buffers hold data for microseconds and discard 99.99% of it, so nobody refreshes them. Add a NOREF(range, lifetime) command: the OS or runtime marks rows whose data will be overwritten or discarded within ~30 ms (activations, framebuffers, network rings, attention scratch), and the DRAM leaves them out of internal refresh. Reading a row past its declared lifetime returns a poison flag.
why: In AI workloads a large share of the footprint is short-lived. Skipping its refresh cuts refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) in proportion, and lets those regions use weak-retention cells (fact 3).

title: Intermittent-IoT rebuild: refresh-free weights refetched from flash on CRC fail
idea: Energy-harvesting IoT nodes let volatile state die and rebuild it from nonvolatile checkpoints. Apply that to immutable LLM weights: refresh the weight region only every 1-4 s (most cells retain seconds), give each 4 KB page a CRC-32 checked on read, and silently re-DMA any failing page from the golden copy on SSD or flash. This needs a per-region refresh-interval register.
why: Weights are ~50-80% of inference memory. Cutting their refresh 16-64x removes most refresh power and bandwidth for that footprint, and lets weight memory use retention-reject dies (fact 3).

title: Mars-rover autonomy: on-die repair agent remaps rows without the host
idea: Mars rovers repair faults on their own because Earth is 20 light-minutes away. Put a tiny state-machine agent and a 1-4K-entry CAM in the DRAM periphery or HBM base die. The agent watches on-die ECC syndromes, judges when a row or column is degrading, copies it to a spare during refresh slots and redirects its address. Repairs are reversible and continue for the whole life of the part, not just once at test.
why: In-field degradation (VRT, aging, hammer damage) turns into silent sparing. Dies with marginal rows can ship, giving ~2-5% yield and a several-fold cut in field DIMM replacements (facts 3, 9).

title: Railway diverse redundancy: ECC parity stored in different physics
idea: SIL-4 railway signalling uses diverse channels so that no single cause can fail both. Keep data in the DRAM dies but store its ECC parity in SRAM or oxide-transistor gain cells on the HBM base die or logic die. Heat-driven retention collapse, a row-hammer burst or a die-level defect then cannot corrupt data and parity together.
why: Common-mode failures are what defeat ECC. With parity stored in a different technology, simpler codes cover correlated faults, permitting weaker DRAM cells and lighter hammer mitigation; the 12.5% of DRAM bits that held parity also become data (facts 1, 9).

title: Venus-lander electronics: SiC access transistors for refresh-free cells
idea: NASA's SiC JFET circuits have run for weeks at 460 C because SiC's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^19 times lower than silicon's. Bond a thin 4H-SiC (or beta-Ga2O3) access-transistor layer onto a silicon periphery wafer, so each cell's off-state leakage is in the attoamps and retention lasts minutes to hours even at 125 C.
why: Attacks the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) beyond the IGZO prior work, and holds up at high temperature, where IGZO is weaker. Refresh nearly disappears and Cs could drop ~5x (fact 1).

title: Pacemaker hibernation: stop refresh, decode the decay on wake
idea: Implants live on microwatts by sleeping. In deep sleep, turn refresh fully off for seconds to minutes and let the retention tail decay. On wake, a page-level BCH/LDPC code (6-8% overhead, sized for the expected tail at that sleep length and temperature) reconstructs every page before use, so no backing store is needed.
why: Refresh and self-refresh are 16-33% of idle power (fact 3). Zero-refresh sleep plus decode-on-wake removes most of it for phones, laptops and parked servers.

title: Fighter-jet limp-home: weak rows twin-pair into differential 2T2C
idea: Combat aircraft fall back to a limp-home mode instead of failing outright. Rows that fail retention or hammer screening are paired with a neighbour row and sensed differentially as one true-plus-complement 2T2C row, halving their capacity but doubling signal, instead of using up spare rows or scrapping the die. Pairing is set per row by fuse or runtime register.
why: Spare rows run out first on weak dies. Twin-pairing rescues dies with many weak rows and lets fabs run thinner capacitors with selective rescue: several points of yield (facts 1, 3).

title: $1-IoT repairless DRAM: no fuses, no spares, a bad-row map
idea: Ultra-cheap IoT parts cannot afford repair. Remove laser and e-fuse repair, spare rows and columns, and the repair test insertion from the die. Instead, store the bad-row list measured at test in a tiny OTP block that the host reads at boot, and map around those rows in page tables.
why: Repair circuitry, fuses and repair test cost periphery area (fact 7: periphery is ~49%) and tester time. That saves ~3-5% die area and one test step per die, with the OS managing the holes.

title: QLC-flash logic for DRAM: half-height capacitors plus LDPC
idea: QLC NAND ships cells with raw BER around 10^-2 because LDPC corrects them. Build DRAM with capacitors at half the height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) and a raw BER near 10^-5, and put a 10-15%-overhead quasi-cyclic LDPC decoder, with a fast hard-decision first pass, in the HBM or CXL logic die so the external error rate meets spec.
why: Halving capacitor aspect ratio cuts the hardest etch and deposition steps and allows a tighter pitch (fact 1). Expect ~15-25% lower cost per bit after paying for parity and the decoder.

title: Defense-grade beachhead: large-cell rad-tolerant DRAM in US mature fabs
idea: Satellites, missiles and nuclear plants pay 10-100x per bit for radiation-tolerant memory. Build a 28-40 nm-class DRAM with large capacitors (~15-25 fF), on-die ECC and hammer-immune row spacing in an underused U.S. mature-node fab, funded by defense and space demand. Then move the same line and team toward commercial nodes.
why: Attacks U.S. manufacturability (1-2% world share) and capital intensity: no EUV, depreciated tools, and a high-margin reliability niche that pays for the learning curve (fact 4).

title: Fleet-proven spec: JEDEC grade with percentile error limits and mandatory ECC
idea: Hyperscaler field studies show real DRAM errors come from a small minority of cells. Create a JEDEC grade that states retention and hammer specs as percentiles (e.g., at most 1e-6 of cells may fail at 64 ms and 85 C) and requires system ECC, instead of demanding that every cell meet the worst case.
why: The worst 1e-6 tail sets refresh and capacitor height today. Percentile specs let vendors ship dies that are now scrapped or downbinned and trim guardbands: ~5-10% yield plus capacitor relief (facts 1, 3).

title: IceCube field updates: microcode-programmable on-die ECC decoder
idea: IceCube's sensors, frozen into Antarctic ice since 2010, receive firmware updates as new failure modes appear. Make on-die ECC a small programmable decoder, with code tables and a syndrome-to-action lookup in SRAM. Vendors can then push new codes, new bit interleaving and new hammer responses to deployed DRAM as a signed mode-register firmware load.
why: New error mechanisms (hammer at ~1k activations, new VRT modes) currently force respins or extra margin. Updatable decoding lets earlier, weaker silicon ship and stay safe (fact 9).

title: Exascale checkpoint inside DRAM: RowClone shadow rows for rollback
idea: Exascale machines survive frequent faults through checkpoints. Add an in-DRAM SNAPSHOT command that copies a row to a shadow row in a reserved subarray by bitline copy (~90 ns, no bus traffic). When an uncorrectable error hits, the runtime rolls back to the shadow copy instead of killing the job.
why: Detected-uncorrectable errors become cheap rollbacks, so DRAM can run weaker codes or cells at higher uncorrectable rates, and checkpoint traffic to NVMe shrinks (facts 5, 8).

title: Starlink lifetime matching: 5-year DRAM with higher stored charge
idea: Starlink satellites deorbit after ~5 years, so their parts need not last 25. AI accelerators also retire in 4-5 years, so specify HBM for a 5-year life and spend the freed dielectric and oxide reliability margin on ~10-15% higher cell storage voltage and wordline overdrive. Each cell then stores more charge with the same capacitor.
why: TDDB and BTI guardbands for a 10-year life cap voltages today. Trading them for 15-25% more stored charge (Q=CV) eases the capacitor charge wall without raising aspect ratio and shrinks the retention tail (facts 1, 10).

title: Scratched-CD codes: cross-interleaved 2D product codes over each mat
idea: Car CD players survived scratches through CIRC, two Reed-Solomon codes crossed by interleaving. Apply a row-by-column product code over each 512x512 mat, so a whole failed wordline or bitline (a burst) is corrected by the orthogonal code during scrub instead of needing a fused spare.
why: Wordline and bitline defects and hammer clusters use up repair resources and yield. A 2D code corrects whole-line failures for ~6% overhead, cutting redundancy area and raising yield (facts 7, 9).

title: Tick-to-trade speculation: use data before strong ECC finishes
idea: High-frequency trading systems act on market data before full validation and unwind on the rare error. Inside the host memory controller, forward the raw 64 B line at normal latency while a heavier decoder (two-symbol-correcting Reed-Solomon over a burst pair) runs in the background. If it disagrees, the core replays dependent instructions through its existing branch-mispredict machinery. Standard DDR5/HBM bursts carry exactly the same bits.
why: Strong ECC normally adds 5-10 ns of latency, so vendors lean on stronger cells instead. Hiding decode latency enables chipkill-class correction on every access and tolerates ~10x weaker raw cell populations at no latency cost (facts 1, 3).

title: Coal-mine canaries: deliberately weak sentinel rows in every subarray
idea: Fabricate 2-4 canary rows per subarray with ~30% less capacitance, so they fail first as temperature, aging or hammer stress rises. The DRAM's internal logic samples them during standard REF slots. When canaries flip, it quietly spends extra internal refreshes on that subarray, the same way TRR already does, all within the unchanged DDR5/HBM REF protocol.
why: Replaces worst-case static guardbands with measured margin, so arrays can run close to their real retention and hammer limits: roughly 1.5-2x looser design margin for <0.1% area (facts 3, 9).

title: Overclocker binning in reverse: weak-retention dies sold as refresh-class parts
idea: Overclockers profile each module's true margins and tune timings to match. Do the reverse for retention: dies that fail 64 ms but pass 32 ms get a 'refresh class' written into vendor bytes of the standard SPD, and the BIOS sets the controller's existing programmable tREFI or 2x-refresh mode to suit.
why: Retention-fail dies are scrapped or burn spare rows today. Selling them as 2x-refresh parts for lightly loaded or cool servers recovers several percent of wafer output (fact 3).

title: Red-team defense: keyed, re-randomized row scrambling inside the DRAM
idea: Treat the row-hammer attacker as the extreme user. Inside each subarray, the DRAM maps logical rows to physical rows through a lightweight keyed permutation (a 4-round Feistel on the row bits). The key is re-drawn at each boot and rotated gradually by background migration during self-refresh, so attackers cannot learn which rows are physical neighbours. External addressing and timing stay standard.
why: Targeted hammering depends on knowing the neighbours. Randomizing them turns attacks into low-odds guessing, so vendors can tolerate cells that flip near 1k activations without heavy per-row counters (fact 9).

title: Exascale ABFT: checksum rows riding inside weight matrices
idea: Million-core supercomputers use Huang-Abraham algorithm-based fault tolerance. Append a checksum row and column to every weight and activation tile, so each GEMM on the accelerator detects and corrects single corrupted elements in the operands it just read from HBM, for ~1-3% extra FLOPs. HBM devices and protocol are untouched.
why: End-to-end correction covers weak on-die ECC, so accelerators can use lower-grade HBM dies or switch off sideband ECC and reclaim its ~3-12% of capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6).

title: Data-parallel training: model replicas become each other's ECC
idea: In a 10,000-GPU job, every data-parallel rank holds identical weights. Periodically checksum each 2 MB weight shard, compare checksums across replicas over NVLink or InfiniBand, and repair any mismatched shard by copying it from a majority peer. Local HBM errors are then corrected by replication that already exists.
why: Weights are ~30-50% of training HBM. Cross-replica voting gives TMR-like protection for free and lets weight regions run on weaker dies or relaxed refresh (facts 3, 6).

title: Battle-short mode: zero out uncorrectable AI weights and keep running
idea: A military 'battle short' bypasses protective trips during combat. In AI inference, when the controller reports a poisoned (uncorrectable) line from a weight region, the runtime substitutes zeros or the per-channel mean for those 32 FP16 values and keeps going instead of raising a machine check. It logs the address so the page can be reloaded later.
why: Neural nets tolerate dropout-like loss of a few weights. Removing the crash penalty lets weight memory run on cheaper dies at higher uncorrectable-error rates (facts 3, 6).

title: Long-context KV triage: low-attention tokens live on relaxed-refresh ranks
idea: Million-token KV caches are among the most extreme memory users. Track each token's cumulative attention score and migrate the bottom ~70% of tokens' K/V blocks onto ranks the controller runs at 4x longer tREFI, or onto retention-weak binned DIMMs. High-attention tokens stay on standard ranks, and errors in rarely attended tokens barely move outputs.
why: The KV cache dominates long-context serving memory. Relaxing refresh on most of it saves refresh power and bandwidth and creates demand for weak bins (fact 3).

title: $1-IoT free ECC: compress each line to make room for parity
idea: Cheap IoT and phone LPDDR has no ECC pins. The host controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta, zero and FP-pattern schemes succeed on ~70-90% of lines) and stores a SEC-DED or BCH code in the freed bits, tracked by one marker bit per line in a small metadata table. Standard non-ECC x16 parts gain protection on most lines.
why: Brings ECC to billions of non-ECC devices without the 12.5% extra chips, so phone and IoT DRAM can tolerate weaker cells and longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Multi-tenant cloud quarantine: tenants own whole subarrays plus guard rows
idea: Treat the hostile cloud tenant as the extreme user. Using the vendor's published row-to-subarray map, the hypervisor gives each VM whole subarrays (hammer disturbance does not cross the sense-amp stripe) and leaves a guard row at any shared boundary. Hammering then only disturbs the attacker's own data.
why: Removes cross-tenant hammer risk, so cells that flip at low activation counts can be used without expensive in-DRAM counters, at <1% guard overhead (fact 9).

title: Recommender hot rows: replicate embedding rows across banks to dilute activations
idea: Recommendation models with Zipf-skewed embedding lookups hit a few rows millions of times per second. The runtime keeps per-row activation counts in a Misra-Gries sketch and replicates the hottest rows into 4-8 banks, round-robining reads so no physical row crosses the hammer threshold. Bank parallelism also raises bandwidth.
why: Workload-driven hammering is what forces conservative cells. Dilution keeps per-row activations under ~1k for ~0.1% capacity overhead (fact 9).

title: Natick-style fail-in-place pods: sealed nitrogen memory sleds, never serviced
idea: Microsoft's sealed undersea datacenter had one-eighth the server failure rate of a land control group and was never touched by technicians. Build sealed, dry-nitrogen DDR5 memory sleds overprovisioned by 15% with rank sparing. The controller retires failing DIMMs in place, and the sled is swapped only at 5-year end of life.
why: Eliminates service labor and lets operators deploy lower-bin DIMMs, because spares absorb their failures. That cuts cost per usable bit by ~5-10% at fleet scale.

title: Proof-of-work logic: speculative-decoding drafts run from junk DRAM
idea: Crypto miners shrug off memory errors because every result is cheaply verified. Host LLM speculative-decoding draft models and their caches on retention-reject or relaxed-refresh DIMMs: the full model's verification pass rejects any token a memory error corrupted, so the only cost is a slightly lower acceptance rate.
why: Creates a productive market for weak-bin DRAM (several percent of output) and frees premium HBM for the target model (fact 3).

title: Deep-space image downlinks: ECC bits spent only on high-order bits
idea: Space probes protect image headers and coarse coefficients far more heavily than fine detail. The host controller repurposes the standard 8 ECC bits per 64-bit beat into a double-error-correcting code over only the sign, exponent and high bits of BF16/INT8 values, leaving low bits unprotected. The DIMM or HBM still stores 72 bits per beat; only the encoder changes.
why: For AI data, low-bit errors are harmless, so concentrating parity roughly triples correction where it matters and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER (relaxed refresh, weak bins) at no capacity cost (fact 3).

title: Genome-coverage redundancy: reclaim ECC lanes as data for self-protected pages
idea: Sequencers keep 30x-redundant reads, so single flips do not matter. On ECC DIMMs and HBM, the OS marks pages that are already protected end-to-end (erasure-coded objects, checksummed caches, FEC'd media, replicated weights), and the controller uses the 8 ECC bits per beat on those pages as data, exposing 12.5% more capacity.
why: Turns up to 12.5% of installed ECC capacity into usable bits on eligible pages. At fleet scale that is new supply without new wafers.

title: Hubble's corrective optics: MRDIMM buffers build stronger codewords on-module
idea: Hubble was fixed after launch by inserting corrective optics (COSTAR). Do the same in the data buffers of standard MRDIMM/LRDIMM modules: the buffers spread each host access across two ranks and compute a longer chipkill-plus symbol code on-module. Part of the second rank holds the extra parity, and the module is sold at lower capacity. The host still sees standard DDR5 timing and ECC lanes.
why: Modules built from sub-spec or high-BER dies present spec-grade reliability to unchanged hosts, making ~5-10% more dies sellable (facts 3, 7).

title: Refurb-phone economy: second-life server DIMMs behind CXL with host codes
idea: Refurbishers in emerging markets turn worn parts into working phones. Harvest DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs from decommissioned servers, re-screen them, and mount them in CXL Type-3 expanders whose controller adds stronger chipkill-plus codes and patrol scrub. Hyperscalers get a cold memory tier at a fraction of new-DIMM cost.
why: Adds supply without wafers. Millions of DIMMs are shredded every year, and reuse with stronger codes for aged cells could cover 5-15% of cold-tier demand (capital and scarce-resource intensity).

title: Desert solar thermal swings: thermal-cycling screen flushes out VRT cells
idea: Desert electronics see 50 C daily swings that expose latent defects. Add a fast package test that cycles dies between -10 C and 95 C several times while repeatedly retention-testing them, pushing variable-retention-time cells into their leaky state so they are repaired before shipment. Nothing at the interface changes.
why: VRT cells escape single-pass tests and later force fleet-wide conservative refresh. Catching them early cuts field errors and supports ~1.5x looser refresh guardbands (fact 3).

title: Cold-boot attacker insight: store each line in its discharge-safe polarity
idea: Cold-boot attackers know DRAM decays toward each cell's ground state. The host controller learns each row's true-cell or anti-cell polarity with a boot-time decay scan, then inverts each 64 B line so most cells hold the discharged state, which cannot leak away. One flag bit per line rides in spare ECC or metadata bits.
why: Real data is zero-heavy. Minimizing charged cells cuts retention and hammer error exposure by ~2-4x on the same silicon (facts 3, 9).

title: Under-hood automotive: phase-change heat spreaders clip DIMM thermal spikes
idea: Automotive ECUs ride out engine heat soak with thermal mass. Fill DIMM and HBM heat spreaders with a phase-change material that melts near 80 C (paraffin blend or Ga-In-Sn alloy), so it absorbs workload bursts and keeps DRAM under the 85 C point where retention halves and 2x refresh kicks in.
why: Avoids doubled refresh (bandwidth and energy) and retention-tail failures during bursts, and lets marginal retention bins operate safely (fact 3).

title: NICU-style first days: field burn-in under mirroring replaces burn-in ovens
idea: Neonatal ICUs watch newborns most closely in the first days, because that is when failures cluster. Ship DRAM without the multi-hour burn-in step. Server BIOS runs new DIMMs in standard memory-mirroring mode with aggressive patrol scrub for the first ~72 hours, retires any infant-mortality failures, then releases full capacity.
why: Burn-in ovens and test time are a real slice of DRAM back-end capital. Moving infant screening into the field cuts test capex and cycle time by ~10-20% (fact 4).

title: Hyperscale error fingerprints: a CVE-style exchange for DRAM failure signatures
idea: The largest fleets log billions of DIMM-hours. Create an industry exchange where operators and vendors share anonymized correctable-error spatial fingerprints (bank, row and column patterns per die lot). Host controllers use them to predict which pages will go uncorrectable and retire them early, and vendors adjust screening by lot.
why: Predictive retirement makes dies with higher raw error rates safe to deploy and could cut DIMM replacements ~30-50%, lifting usable supply and tightening yield feedback to fabs (facts 3, 9).

title: Dead-die HBM stacks: GPU remaps around dead channels, stacks still ship
idea: Treat HBM stacking yield as the extreme case. A stack with one defective die is normally scrapped after the costly stacking step. Instead, sell it as a 7/8-capacity part: its SPD-style descriptor lists the dead die's pseudo-channels, and the GPU memory controller compacts its address map around them over the unchanged HBM interface.
why: HBM stacking yield loss of 20-30% is mostly wasted good silicon (fact 6). Recovering even half of single-die-defect stacks raises effective HBM supply by ~10%.
